What happens when the DOM can go anywhere a pixel can?

Experiments and drop-in libraries built on the HTML-in-canvas API. A <canvas> draws live child elements in 2D, WebGL or WebGPU while they keep taking clicks, typing, text selection and accessibility.

Chrome 157+ ships HTML-in-canvas on desktop and Android (this site also sends an Origin Trial token for Chrome 148 to 156; how to check or enable it). Without it, every page here shows as plain HTML. Started as a <slot> experiment by Paul Kinlan: read the story.

Examples

Twenty-nine highlights of what HTML-in-canvas can do. In every picture, the UI is live HTML drawn by a canvas and you can interact with it.

Per-element themes

Twenty-nine skins (glass, stained glass, clay, thermal, LED board, comic, X-ray, oscilloscope) wrapped round each element of a live form.

Peel this page back to read its HTML

One canvas draws the whole page. Drag the turned top-right corner and the page rolls back like paper to reveal the HTML the server sent.

Conveyor belt virtualised list

An endless list built from ten live DOM rows, drawn round two 3D rollers with checkboxes and buttons that still work as they roll by.

A lens that translates

Drag a live lens over an article to translate, simplify or summarise only the words under it while editing the original text keeps working.

Fragment shaders on elements

fx="ripple" draws an element through a fragment shader. CSS custom properties set the uniforms, and you can supply your own GLSL or WGSL.

A magnifier over live DOM

Fifteen lenses. The area under the lens is drawn again at the lens zoom, so 4px text stays sharp, and clicks and typing pass through.

Forms on a simulated mesh

Forms drawn on jelly, cloth and paper meshes. Hit testing follows the mesh, so a click reaches the control under the pointer.

Form controls drawn as instruments

Real radio buttons arranged round a rotary dial, faders and gauges drawn by a canvas while keeping keyboard navigation and form values.

Curved range sliders and input pickers

Five more input pickers, starting with a real <input type="range"> drawn in 3px slices round an arc with a live <output> in the middle.

Form controls in a drawn setting

Skewed inputs and checkboxes wired to drawn callout lines that update live from the browser's own constraint validation state.

Shader uniforms written in CSS only

Twelve cards drawn through one shader whose uniforms come from CSS keyframes, typed attr(), random() and if(). Edit any card's CSS live.

A select whose picker is drawn by a canvas

The options of a customisable <select> are drawn as a wheel, fisheye list, radial menu, 3D carousel, hand of cards or helix while keeping the value and keyboard.

Date, time and colour pickers in a canvas

A clock, a calendar and a ring of swatches replace the built-in pickers of three ordinary inputs. Every hour and day is a real button.

A datalist drawn by a canvas

The <datalist> of a text input is moved into a canvas in a popover. Its options draw as a list or pills and rearrange as you type.

Transitions between two live states

Shatter, fold and burn transitions drawn in WebGPU or WebGL. Both states accept input during the transition, and it can be held part way.

Text drawn glyph by glyph

Each letter of a paragraph is a particle. The paragraph stays one element, so selection, find-in-page, links and editing keep working.

A form in a three.js scene

A form used as a texture on a laptop screen, a billboard and a curved wall. Typing, Tab and text selection work on all three.

HTML panels in WebXR

HTML panels in a three.js XR scene. Controller rays become pointer events on the elements. Includes a desktop preview and a headset emulator.

A zoomable board of documents

Each tile is an element or a same-origin iframe drawn under a zoom transform. Text is rasterised again at each zoom level, up to 800%.

DOM elements inside Rust egui and Qt Quick

Real HTML inputs, selects and spellcheck textareas hosted inside WebAssembly egui and Qt Quick canvases, with working window occlusion.

Cassette deck from audio controls

A tactile cassette deck with spinning reels and a glowing counter built out of real audio controls drawn into one canvas.

HTML overlays on video

A caption bar, a poll and a ticker in HTML over a video, in one canvas. Record it with sound, export frame by frame, or send it over WebRTC.

Record and replay DOM frames

A ring buffer of frames of an element. Drag the slider to scrub earlier frames, replay the last five seconds, or restore an earlier form state.

One element streamed to a phone

Scan a code and one panel of the page is on your phone over WebRTC. Taps and typing on the phone are sent back and applied to the element.

Widgets moved into another window

Pull a widget into a popup, an always-on-top window, another tab or another origin. What you do there happens to the element on this page.

Picture-in-picture for any element

pipElement(el) puts an element in a window above your other windows: moved there, as a live picture that takes input, or as a video.

Share one panel of a page

Send one panel to a support agent or a vision model instead of your whole screen. Private fields are blacked out before the frame is sent.

Cross-origin widgets without an iframe box

A price and a product card from another origin, laid out inline in a blog post. The other origin asks the reader before it sends any pixels.

Export an element as PNG or video

captureElement(el) wraps an element in a canvas for one frame and returns a PNG. The same library records video and prints at 300 DPI.

Quick start with <canvas-slot> one module, no dependencies 
<script type="module" src="https://html-in-canvas.page/lib/canvas-slot.js"></script>

<canvas-slot id="stage">
  <h2 slot="title">A heading</h2>
  <button slot="cta">A button you can press</button>
</canvas-slot>

<script type="module">
  const stage = document.getElementById('stage');   // the <canvas-slot> element

  // draw(slotName, x, y) is drawElementImage() for the element in that slot.
  stage.onrender = ({ ctx, draw, time }) => {
    ctx.rotate(Math.sin(time / 800) * 0.05);
    draw('title', 20, 20);
    draw('cta', 20, 90);
  };
</script>

Limits of the API

I kept running into the same four limits, and most of the code on this site is shaped by them. The tests behind each one are in FINDINGS.md, the friction log and the crash list.

  • The element has to be a descendant of the canvas. There's no way to draw an element by reference. The slot pages use a shadow root to get round this.
  • An element has one hit-test region. If it's drawn twice, or in pieces, only one position receives input. The portal, lens and transition pages move the region to the pointer.
  • An ElementImage draws only into its source canvas. To show an element in another document, the pages send pixels and forward input events back.
  • An element that isn't drawn can still take focus. Tab reaches controls you can't see unless the page marks them inert.
